Wiring variations that enable and constrain neural computation in a sensory microcircuit.

First, I take my hat off to the authors for their devoted study of AL circuits using such labor-intensive methods. For this submission, anatomy is the bedrock, while the modeling aspects are more conjectural. In particular, I would submit that the weakest link is the main story line, the link between synaptic structure and synaptic strength. Even so, it ought to be possible to relate all parameters of the connectome to those of the modeling, provided we have all the requisite measures. To this end, the authors provide important data on dendritic caliber, which has generally not been treated extensively in the literature on Drosophila neurons. While it's easy to count synapse number and plot distributions, however, so far missing from the authors' story is synapse size. Does this vary in any consistent way between (pre)synaptic sites, and do the postsynaptic densities, which I presume are also visible, co-vary with the size of presynaptic contact? The size of the dendrite may co-vary with these, but is not itself a proxy for synapse size. If the authors are to claim a relationship between synapses number and the strength of synaptic transmission, I think these additional parameters should be included, and hope they can be mined with relative ease from existing image data, even if I imagine these are all fixed modules.

Introduction, fourth paragraph. Additional important discussion on wiring accuracy in brains is to be found in Takemura et al. (PNAS 112 (Rall, 1964): 13711-13716, 2015) which the authors cite but only later in support of missing cells in medulla columns. The PNAS paper includes reference to comparisons between left/right homologues in C. elegans and comparisons between synapse numbers in neighboring medulla columns in Drosophila both of which bear on the authors' data.

In fact, the medulla analyses indicate the high order of synaptic and wiring accuracy of which Drosophila is also capable in constructing the synaptic circuits in its brain, in that case in the visual system. Accuracy, or invariance, in the case of the latter is presumably driven by the need to transmit reliably at the high temporal frequencies demanded by vision, a requirement that can be less demanding in the olfactory pathway.

'Feedforward' and 'onto' sound to me to be contradictory because feedforward could refer to the synaptic outputs of the cell in question. I think what the authors want to say is "along with all the excitatory inputs (synapses) onto these cells".

"Three experts independently identified glomerulus DM6 in the EM data set by visual inspection based on published light-level maps". The account is remarkable more for what it does not say than what it does say. I find the documentation of how the authors selected DM6 neurons for reconstruction to be insufficient. Although confocal data clearly reveal the antennal lobe's glomerular map, based especially on synaptic and genetic labelling, such data are deceptive for EM studies, which reveal all profiles not their selective features. In particular there are no clear glial boundaries between glomeruli, and glomeruli, which the authors fail to mention, and can only be identified unambiguously with reference to the map of surrounding glomeruli, or possibly from Cartesian coordinates, and I think the authors should acknowledge this. Quite possibly the authors have gained sufficient expertise from physiological recordings to identify specific glomeruli but this is in the intact living antennal lobe. Glomeruli also partly overlap each other in the depth of the lobe neuropile. Moreover, we are not told why DM6 itself was chosen over other glomeruli, and as a rationale the authors may want to cite their own physiological studies. These questions are central to the authors' analysis and should be made clear in the text, because while I am sure that great care was taken, and we can be reassured that three experts made the same identification, in fact it's not a trivial problem at all at EM level. Most readers would not know or understand this because confocal maps are so convincing, because most readers never see EM, and because most may erroneously assume that there is a clear glial boundary surrounding each glomerulus. It's also quite possible to target DM6 in a living prep, which studies from the Wilson lab have done repeatedly, but the contours of the antennal lobe's surface also differ from the 2D images from EM sections. These issues of 'why' and 'how' need to be clearly addressed. The text of the Methods should enable another worker to repeat the authors' observations. In particular, how can the authors provide the reader the clear assurance that they have actually targeted the same glomerulus on left and right sides of the brain, and that the left/right asymmetries they find are not the outcome of choosing different glomeruli on the two sides. I fully accept, by contrast, that the authors scrupulously identify in the EM dataset ORNs and PNs from their respective arbors and axon trajectories.

Figure 1A. Related: although valuable as an EM overview, Figure 1A provides insufficient information to identify DM6, especially in the z axis. Was the entire glomerulus reconstructed and how did the authors decide where its boundaries lay?

Orphans: To what does the rate of orphans refer? The number of independent fragments that were presynaptic to PNs but could not be connected to an identified cell? How many synapses did these contribute? Were any orphaned at both ends, having no contact with either identified ORN or PN? If so, what proportion?

The claim (subsection “Cells comprising the glomerular micro-circuit”, last paragraph) that false continuations between fragments are easily detected and corrected during independent review is more likely to be an attribute of the arbor than of the reconstruction strategy, since larval neurons in Drosophila tend to have relatively more stout neurites with distal extremities that bear most synapses. Thus, the conclusion that they are therefore very rare in the final reconstruction may be less warranted than is claimed.

Presynaptic T-bars. Please comment on the range of structural phenotypes exhibited by presynaptic T-bars in Figure 1— – figure supplement 3, or from the authors' analysis of synapses in serial sections.

Table 1. Subsection “Relative abundance of connection types”, first paragraph. I do not find Table 1, which is needed to interpret Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

Synaptic numbers, subsection “The structure and strength of excitatory connections”. Documentation of synapse numbers is good, and interpretation is generally appropriate, but the authors should review their text carefully to check the tendency to equate synapse number with synapse strength, and to distinguish semantic reference to these two strictly. It's also important to remember the processing depth introduced by feedback synapses, for which transmission gain reflects not only the number of feedforward synapses but also upstream synapses. Thus, in addition to the gain of individual synapses, feedback circuits inherit the signal gain from their synaptic inputs.

Adjacency matrix in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 resembles a number of such matrices that have now been published, with the top numbers around 50 synapses, in line with those in other brain regions, which the authors could indicate. Each intercept represents the site of presumed transmission between a single pre- and postsynaptic neuron, but the text should acknowledge that because each presynaptic site has several postsynaptic elements, a number of intercepts in the matrix necessarily are coordinately linked. In fact, I find no easy metric for synaptic divergence revealed in this figure, or elsewhere in the text. How many dyads, triads etc. are incorporated in the matrix. Alternatively, how many monads?

Related to the preceding point: Figure 1—figure supplement 3. These are single images of synapses that fail to reveal profiles above and below the plane of section. Yet clearly there are multiple dendrites at single release sites, as can indeed be seen in some sections. This information is given in Figure 4——figure supplement 1E but only as averages that compare Ipsi and Contra ORNs.

The authors state that "All synaptic conductance events had the same size and shape." This presumably assumes that those conductance events were shared at the same presynaptic site? Do the authors imagine that each postsynaptic dendrite sees the same cloud of neurotransmitter release, or is the cloud shared amongst the several dendrites. If that number varies, does this mean that transmission varies with the number of dendrites, or is the dendritic signal unaltered; how does the outcome affect the authors' modeling? I don't think there is an easy answer, but these issues should at least be acknowledged, and as far as possible discussed.

Figure 1—figure supplement 4. In addition, I find that using black for 0 synapses is confusing, not least because I find it hard to discriminate differences in tone for dark intercepts having few synapses, and recommend replotting this matrix using white for intercepts having 0 synapses. Alternatively, reverse the entire spectrum of tones, so that 50+ is black and 0 is white.

Methods. Of the 1917 sections cut, we are told, in the subsection “Large-scale TEM imaging and alignment”, how many sections were lost, apparently 145, from 1 to 6, about 7% of the total series – so roughly equal to the number of orphans, but not how many sections were needed to encompass the DM6 glomeruli, and thus not therefore what proportion of those were drops. Losing 6 sections (0.3µm) is very damaging to the continuity of any series, but at least the authors are honest in reporting them. How many of these drops accounted for the occurrence of orphans, one wonders, and were these equal on left and right DN6 sides? The authors should I think try to address these points.

results.result: The authors collected a large-scale EM dataset of the anterior Drosophila brain comprising 1917 thin sections at 4×4 nm²/pixel resolution, totaling 4 million images and 50 TB of data, covering both left and right antennal lobes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 provide consistent technical specifications for the EM dataset. The imaging parameters, data volume, and spatial coverage are clearly stated and represent standard methodology for serial section EM reconstruction studies.

results.result: The DM6 glomerulus is innervated by 53 ORNs (27 left, 26 right), with two ORNs projecting only ipsilaterally, resulting in 52 ORNs per glomerulus. Three PNs were found on the left and two on the right.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C8 describe the cellular composition of the reconstructed circuit based on direct EM observations. The counts are internally consistent (53 total ORNs minus 2 unilateral = 52 per glomerulus) and represent primary data from the reconstruction.

results.result: PN number varies between left and right DM6 glomeruli with no consistent lateralization bias. This variability represents true biological variation rather than Gal4 expression artifacts, consistent with cell number variation observed in other Drosophila neural networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11 and C82-C86 are supported by both EM reconstruction data and photoactivation experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The finding is contextualized with prior literature on optic lobe variability (C83-C84), strengthening the interpretation that cell number variation is a general phenomenon in Drosophila.

results.result: Reconstruction completeness was high, with orphan fragments representing only 6.8±1.5% overall (4.4±0.8% left, 10.4±0.4% right).
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13 provide quality metrics for the reconstruction. The low orphan percentage indicates good reconstruction quality, though the left-right asymmetry suggests some regional variation in data quality. These are standard quality control metrics for connectomics studies.

results.result: ORNs deliver ~33% of output to PNs and most of the remainder to multiglomerular neurons. PNs receive ~75% of input from ORNs and ~20% from multiglomerular neurons, while devoting ~90% of their output to multiglomerular neurons. All PNs connect reciprocally with sister PNs.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C22 describe the connectivity patterns observed in the reconstruction (Figure 1E-F). The percentages are directly measured from synapse counts. The reciprocal PN-PN connectivity (C22) is consistent with prior electrophysiology, providing cross-validation.

results.result: Unitary ORN→PN connections contain ~23 synapses on average, producing ~5 mV uEPSPs. PN→PN connections contain ~11 synapses, while ORN→ORN and PN→ORN connections typically have 1-2 synapses. These values agree with prior electrophysiological and optical measurements.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C27 report synapse counts from EM reconstruction (Figure 1G) and compare them to prior physiological measurements (C24-C25). The agreement between EM counts and functional predictions from quantal analysis validates both approaches.

results.result: Each ORN T-bar contacts multiple postsynaptic profiles (typically one PN and 1-2 non-PN profiles). T-bar size correlates strongly with the number of postsynaptic profiles and weakly with postsynaptic contact area.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 describe the ultrastructural organization of individual synapses based on detailed measurements (Figure 1—figure supplement 5-6). The correlations are statistically significant and represent standard polyadic synapse architecture in Drosophila.

results.result: Right PNs have larger dendrites than left PNs, but total ORN→PN synapses per glomerulus are similar. Individual right PNs receive 53% more ORN synapses, resulting in similar synapse density. Right PNs also receive more multiglomerular neuron input and form more output synapses.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C35 describe compensatory scaling between cell number, dendrite size, and synapse number (Figure 2). The measurements are internally consistent: fewer PNs on the right correlates with larger dendrites and more synapses per PN, maintaining constant total synapses per glomerulus.

results.result: Compartmental modeling reveals that despite differences in dendrite size and synapse number, right and left PNs have nearly identical somatic uEPSP amplitudes. This results from compensatory effects: right PNs have smaller mEPSPs (due to lower input resistance and greater dendritic attenuation) but more synapses per connection.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C42 present results from compartmental models constrained by EM reconstructions and electrophysiological parameters (Figure 3). The models demonstrate precise compensation between anatomical parameters. The modeling approach is well-established and appropriately applied.

results.result: When one PN is missing, remaining PNs grow larger dendrites and receive proportionally more synapses, resulting in equal average responses to ORN spikes. This compensatory mechanism is consistent with homeostatic plasticity observed in other systems and the instructive role of PN dendrites in development.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C98 synthesize current observations with prior studies on homeostatic plasticity (C93-C95) and developmental mechanisms (C97-C98). The compensation is demonstrated through both anatomical measurements and modeling (C89, C92). The proposed developmental scenario (C96) is speculative but well-supported by cited literature.

results.result: PNs receive 35% more synapses from ipsilateral than contralateral ORNs, providing a structural basis for the 30-40% stronger ipsilateral connections observed electrophysiologically. Compartmental models predict 27% stronger ipsilateral uEPSPs, with no systematic differences in synapse placement or ORN axon length.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C50 link behavioral observations (odor lateralization, C43-C44) to prior electrophysiology (C45) to current EM data (C46) and modeling (C47). The quantitative agreement between predicted (27%) and observed (30-40%) ipsi-contra differences validates the structural explanation. The systematic difference in synapse number (C46, Figure 4C) is the primary mechanism.

results.result: While the ipsi-contra asymmetry is not perfectly precise at the single connection level, it is sufficiently precise to enable PNs to prefer ipsilateral stimuli when stimuli are sufficiently strong.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 acknowledge variability in the ipsi-contra asymmetry (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) while demonstrating functional sufficiency through modeling. This represents an appropriate assessment of the precision and functional consequences of the observed structural variation.

results.result: The number of synapses per ORN→PN connection varies widely (e.g., 10-36 synapses for different ipsilateral ORNs onto the same PN), with a CV of 0.31. This variation correlates with physical proximity between ORN axons and PN dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 and C99 quantify connection strength variability (Figure 5B-C). The correlation with proximity (C55, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) suggests a developmental mechanism. The CV value (C56) is consistent with prior optical studies, providing cross-validation.

results.result: Despite large variation in synapse number, there is little variation in mean mEPSP amplitude or summation efficacy across connections. Dendritic filtering has a uniform effect across connections because each connection samples many dendritic locations. Thus, synapse number is the major source of connection strength variation.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 and C79-C81 demonstrate through modeling that dendritic filtering effects average out across the multiple synapses comprising each connection (Figure 5D-G). This makes synapse number the dominant variable determining connection strength, a key finding for understanding circuit function.

results.result: Different ORNs from the same antenna have markedly different effects on PN membrane potential (up to 10-fold range), suggesting PNs do not weight ORNs equally and that PN responses are dominated by a fraction of the ORN population.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 are logical inferences from the observed variation in synapse number and the modeling results showing large uEPSP amplitude ranges (Figure 5H). The conclusion that PNs do not equally weight ORNs is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Connection strengths are correlated among ipsilateral sister PNs (7 of 8 comparisons significant, r=0.44-0.78) but not between left and right PNs (0 of 12 comparisons significant). Since all PNs experience identical ORN spike trains, this lack of cross-midline correlation indicates that connection strength variation includes 'connection noise' rather than being optimized to ORN spiking properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C70 present a critical test of whether connection strength variation is adaptive or noisy (Figure 6). The logic is sound: if variation were optimized to ORN properties, it should correlate across all PNs since they receive the same ORN inputs (C65-C66). The absence of cross-midline correlations (C68) despite ipsilateral correlations (C67) supports the connection noise interpretation.

results.result: Connection noise limits PN ability to accurately estimate ORN spike counts. Simulations show that natural connection variability impairs odor detection and lateralization performance, particularly for weak stimuli near perceptual threshold (12 spontaneous spikes in 200 ms).
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 and C102 use classifier simulations to quantify the functional impact of connection noise (Figure 7). The simulations appropriately model the detection task and demonstrate that equalizing synapse numbers improves performance, confirming that natural variability is functionally limiting. The spontaneous spike rate (C73) is measured from prior electrophysiology.

results.result: Synapse number per connection strongly correlates with connection strength. Ipsilateral connections contain 35% more synapses than contralateral connections, and there is no sizeable ipsi-contra difference in synaptic conductance.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 synthesize findings on the structural basis of connection strength. C78 is an inference from the observation that synapse number explains the ipsi-contra difference, but this inference is reasonable given the data. The conclusion that conductance differences are not major contributors is well-supported.

results.result: ORN→PN connections produce simulated uEPSP amplitudes ranging from 1.6 to 10 mV. If all ORNs were functionally identical, this variation would be non-optimal because PN responses would be dominated by a fraction of ORN axons.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 present modeling results (Figure 5H) and their functional interpretation. The conditional statement in C101 ('if all ORNs were functionally identical') is appropriate, acknowledging that the optimality assessment depends on assumptions about ORN function.

results.result: Synapse number variations are correlated among ipsilateral sister PNs but uncorrelated across the midline. This correlated developmental noise may contribute to the high electrical noise correlations observed among ipsilateral sister PNs, which affects the speed and accuracy of odor responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C107 link structural observations to prior electrophysiological findings and functional consequences. The connection between correlated wiring noise and electrical noise correlations (C105) is speculative but reasonable. The functional relevance (C107) is supported by citation to prior work.

results.result: Comparison with larval connectome data reveals that adult ORN→PN connections have fewer synapses (~23 vs ~70) than larval connections, partially compensating for increased ORN number. Adult networks also show more complex control of ORN output, with substantial PN→ORN and ORN→ORN connectivity absent in larvae.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C114 compare adult and larval circuit organization using published larval connectome data. The comparisons are straightforward and the inferences about compensation (C111) and increased complexity (C114) are reasonable. This provides developmental context for the adult findings.

results.result: Systematic variations in synapse number enable specific computations (odor lateralization, response equalization), representing functional capacity. However, unsystematic 'connection noise' represents residual imprecision that limits neural computation, though some imprecision can be balanced by homeostatic mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C121 synthesize the major findings into a conceptual framework distinguishing systematic ('signal') from unsystematic ('noise') wiring variation. This synthesis is well-supported by the data presented throughout the study and appropriately acknowledges both the capabilities and limitations of developmental precision.

results.result: In the optic lobe medulla, the CV of synapse number per connection ranges from 0.08 to 0.87 across different connection types.
results.evaluation: Claim C103 cites prior EM work on the optic lobe, providing comparative context for the connection variability observed in the antennal lobe (CV=0.31). This is a straightforward citation of published data.

results.result: Drosophila melanogaster is likely to be the next organism whose brain is fully mapped at the connectomic level.
results.evaluation: Claim C122 is speculation about future connectomics efforts. While reasonable given ongoing efforts, this is not a scientific result that can be evaluated as supported or unsupported by the current study.
